body:
#### Background
It just so happens over the past couple weeks I have been investigating `ObjectDB` in 3.x with the view of overhauling `ObjectID` and the DB itself. It is just possible that I could look at forward porting the new `ObjectDB`, but I'd prefer to implement in 3.x first, and it would depend whether there was desire to improve `ObjectDB` in terms of 4.x roadmap.

#### `is_instance_valid(obj)`
I hadn't been aware of this API until looking into this area, I spotted it in gdnative / mono. I'm not sure exactly why this API exists (maybe some users of it can enlighten me). It seems better to lookup via opaque `ObjectID` (primary method), looking up by pointer uses e.g. a hashmap and is likely to be slow at best.

Imo closest to the current system the paradigm should be:
```
var obj : Object = instance_from_id(id);
if (obj)
{
... use obj
}
else
{
// invalid
}
```
Without an error message, just return NULL if the ID is invalid. This has one API call compared to your method which is doing 3 separate API calls to get an object and decide whether it is valid.

However, this is still not thread safe, which can be a concern. Really for thread safety you'd want to do something like increment a reference on the object when grabbing it, and prevent it being deleted until that reference was released.

It may be this is prevented by other means, such as `queue_free` only being flushed at a sync point (in 3.x) and the thread guards in 4.x may prevent operations except on main thread (so another thread can't delete if always deleted from main thread). But I'm not super familiar with the behaviour in 4.x.

Access of data within the objects is currently not super thread safe either, but that's a side topic.

## ObjectDB debugging
This is actually a good idea imo, I'll add it to my version if I go further with it (i.e. if the `ObjectID` changes in #107629 get merged), then I can look at going forward with the `ObjectDB` replacement.

The current 4.x `ObjectDB` uses validators in the `ObjectIDs` from memory, so your old approach will likely not work. It probably needs in built support to walk the structure and build some logs.

> If you try "is_instance_id_valid()" on random ids, Godot will then spam this crash condition for absolutely no reasons:

This is actually for good reason, you are feeding an invalid `ObjectID`, and it is detecting the error. `ObjectID` is opaque (i.e. you can't make any assumptions about how it will behave, it could be ID, handle, pointer etc), and your technique is undocumented and only worked by accident in 3.x (and won't work after `ObjectDB` changes).

As to why nothing like this is currently exposed, I can only guess, but it may be because it is internal, and if something is going wrong here (like leaks) it would hopefully become obvious quite quick. But user code could be causing object leaks of course, so I am in agreement some logging / diff API could be useful.

It is interesting to see diffs, but of course for internal object allocations these are subject to change as contributors work on the engine.

Thank you lawnjelly for your answer, I agree on most point you made though, I would like to add some accuracy and some points to this.

First of all, what you are proposing here:
> Imo closest to the current system the paradigm should be:
> 
> ```
> var obj : Object = instance_from_id(id);
> if (obj)
> {
> ... use obj
> }
> else
> {
> // invalid
> }
> ```

is the exact reason I posted  [this issue aka. #55204](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/55204) in November 2021, so we are going back on what we went back in the first place xD (and I have no idea on that anymore because I've been supposedly proven wrong on that subject)



> The current 4.x `ObjectDB` uses validators in the `ObjectIDs` from memory, so your old approach will likely not work. It probably needs in built support to walk the structure and build some logs.

I'm aware of the invalid aspect of this approach, but still Godot needs a way to have an horizontal access to ObjectDB records for debugging purpose, because as of right now the way I understand it, people are just making assumptions on memory leaks rather than checking what create those leaks (which is just a very bad approach from an engineering point of view, we don't estimate memory leaks, we check for them)



> > If you try "is_instance_id_valid()" on random ids, Godot will then spam this crash condition for absolutely no reasons:
> 
> This is actually for good reason, you are feeding an invalid `ObjectID`, and it is detecting the error.

Yes, I see the reason why from the code's point of view, but again from an engineering point of view a validity check should never be invalid by essence.



> your technique is undocumented and only worked by accident in 3.x

The issue with that, is that I love Godot in the first place for being able to check that memory map, this technique has been proven to be the right way for checking memory leaks at the time (sometimes in 2018) because it allows to find them by observability. It cover all cases of unattended behaviour from the engine (which will always happen, to be honest with our approach of Godot, it's normal and perfectly fine if Godot has strong tools to debug the memory)



> As to why nothing like this is currently exposed, it is likely because it is internal, and if something is going wrong here (like leaks) it would hopefully become obvious quite quick.

This is something I can't agree with, Godot's behaviour is **"**obvious**"** when dealing with tens to hundreds of object, but Godot's goal is to make video-games, and video-games, even in very simple case are always likely to have thousands to millions of objects. Video games are almost always the most complicated applications created, and this goes for multiple reasons: it has to manage at least a rendering, an audio, an input, a storage, a memory and a physics engine in 99.99% of cases, all those in real time while keeping peak performances. This is what make video games so special as applications, and this is the reason you can't expect people to always be able to pull a Minimal Reproduction Project for every issue users encounter, and moreover you can't expect issues to still be obvious when a project is going.


Those are the reasons why for me `get_used_instance_ids()` is the way to go, it is the shortest way to access the memory map, it is relatively easy to test if that function is still going well after a change and we don't rely on some prayers that Godot's memory leaks remain obvious.

> As to why nothing like this is currently exposed, it is likely because it is internal, and if something is going wrong here (like leaks) it would hopefully become obvious quite quick.

Yeah to be more clear, I don't want to suggest that it shouldn't be available (indeed as I say I agree it should), just trying to hypothesize some reasoning why it might not have been previously exposed by prior authors. Perhaps I can reword this.

Also often features aren't added simply because there is a policy of waiting for demand, and maybe there hasn't been that demand yet.

> but where is the tool to know what are those objects?

It's here, a very useful feature, I recommend testing it and giving feedback:
- https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/97210

> Where is the function `get_used_instance_ids()` in the `@GlobalScope`?

Such a method would be more suited to the snapshot API, as tracking code usually requires inefficient handling, which we do not want in release template builds. Object snapshotting is absurdly slow in native already, doing it in GDScript sounds like a nightmare, so a built-in snapshot tool is probably a better solution for your use case too.
